text: Fill in the key biochemical terms for these three disorders of lipid handling.
questions: Fatty liver develops when triacylglycerol input exceeds output — output depends on beta-oxidation and export as VLDL, which requires *ApoB-100:Which apolipoprotein must the liver synthesise to assemble and secrete VLDL?*.

In kwashiorkor the liver cannot export enough VLDL because dietary protein is too low to make ApoB-100 and *phosphatidylcholine/lecithin:Besides the apolipoprotein, which phospholipid is needed for the VLDL particle shell?*, so triacylglycerol is trapped in hepatocytes.

Alcohol causes fatty liver by raising the hepatic *NADH:Alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase both generate this reduced cofactor.* to NAD⁺ ratio, which inhibits beta-oxidation and promotes fatty acid esterification.
Cholesterol gallstones form when bile becomes *supersaturated:What term describes a solution holding more solute than it can keep dissolved?* with cholesterol relative to bile salts and phospholipid.
Obesity results from chronic energy surplus: when intake exceeds expenditure, the excess is stored as *triacylglycerol/triglyceride:What is the storage form of fat in adipocytes?* in adipose tissue.

overallFeedback.feedback: All three conditions follow from lipid input exceeding output. In fatty liver, triacylglycerol accumulates because VLDL export is impaired (needs ApoB-100 and phosphatidylcholine — both deficient in protein malnutrition) or because alcohol's high NADH/NAD⁺ ratio blocks oxidation. Cholesterol gallstones crystallise from supersaturated bile. Obesity stores surplus dietary energy as adipose triacylglycerol — each is an input–output mismatch in a different tissue.
